Kaocen flees north and is caught and hanged in Fezzan in 1919.
events.search: Kaocen revolt 1916 1917 Tuareg siege of Agadez Senussi

events.title: The Chemin des Dames and the mutinies, April – June 1917
events.place: The Chemin des Dames ridge, on the Aisne
events.summary: General Nivelle promises to break the German front in two days. On 16 April 1917, French troops attack up the Chemin des Dames ridge, into machine guns that the shelling has left intact. The offensive fails, with over 100,000 French casualties in two weeks. In May and June, soldiers in dozens of divisions refuse to go back to the attack. Pétain replaces Nivelle, gives more leave and better food, waits for the Americans and tanks, and has a few dozen mutineers shot.
events.search: Chemin des Dames Nivelle offensive 1917 French army mutinies

events.title: The Second Battle of the Marne, 15 July – 6 August 1918
events.summary: In the spring of 1918, Germany throws its last forces at the Allied lines and comes back to the Marne. On 15 July it attacks around Reims, but the French are ready. On 18 July, French and American troops led by General Mangin counter-attack from the forest of Villers-Cotterêts with hundreds of tanks. The Germans have to retreat beyond the Vesle. Marshal Foch keeps up the pressure: from now on the Allies advance until the armistice.
events.search: Second Battle of the Marne 1918 Villers-Cotterets counter-attack Foch Chateau-Thierry

events.title: Alsace–Lorraine returns to France, 1918 – 1920
events.summary: Germany had taken Alsace and part of Lorraine from France in 1871. After the armistice, French troops enter Metz on 19 November and Strasbourg on 22 November 1918, to cheering crowds. The Treaty of Versailles returns the land to France on 10 January 1920, and it becomes the departments of Bas-Rhin, Haut-Rhin and Moselle. They keep some of their German-era laws, such as the Concordat on religion, to this day.
events.search: Alsace-Lorraine returns to France 1918 1920 Strasbourg Metz Versailles

events.title: The Battle of Kousséri, 22 April 1900
events.place: On the Chari, near today's N'Djamena
events.summary: Three French columns, one from Algeria across the Sahara, one from Niger and one from the Congo, meet near Lake Chad to fight the warlord Rabih az-Zubayr, who rules the Bornu and the lands south of the lake. At Kousséri, on the Chari, they defeat and kill him; the French commander Major Lamy is killed too. A month later the French found Fort-Lamy, today's N'Djamena, and the military territory of Chad begins.
events.search: Battle of Kousseri 1900 Rabih az-Zubayr Lamy Fort-Lamy conquest of Chad

events.title: Coppolani's "peaceful conquest" of Mauritania, 1902 – 1905
events.place: Trarza, Brakna and Tagant, to Tidjikja
events.summary: North of the Senegal river live the Moorish emirates of Trarza, Brakna, Tagant and Adrar. Xavier Coppolani, a Corsican raised in Algeria who speaks Arabic and knows the Sufi brotherhoods, wins over their emirs and religious leaders one by one, backed by small columns of troops. By 1904 Trarza, Brakna and Tagant have accepted French rule, and France makes Mauritania a territory of its own. Coppolani is killed at Tidjikja in May 1905.
events.search: Xavier Coppolani peaceful conquest Mauritania 1902 1905 Trarza Brakna Tagant Tidjikja

events.title: The Entente Cordiale, 8 April 1904
events.summary: After centuries of rivalry, and only six years after the Fashoda crisis, France and the United Kingdom settle their colonial quarrels. Britain leaves France a free hand in Morocco, and France stops opposing British rule in Egypt. They also share out their claims in Siam, the New Hebrides, West Africa and the Newfoundland fisheries. It is not an alliance, but the two countries draw closer against Germany and fight side by side in 1914.
events.search: Entente Cordiale 1904 France United Kingdom Morocco Egypt

events.title: The Franco-Siamese treaties, 1904 and 1907
events.summary: Siam keeps its independence between British Burma and French Indochina by giving up land. In 1904 it cedes to France Sainyabuli and the land west of the Mekong at Champasak, which go to Laos, and Koh Kong and Mlu Prey, which go to Cambodia. In 1907 it hands over the provinces of Battambang, Siem Reap and Sisophon, which Siam had held since 1795, in exchange for Trat, which French troops had occupied. Cambodia gets back the temples of Angkor.
events.search: Franco-Siamese treaties 1904 1907 Battambang Siem Reap Angkor Sainyabuli Champasak Trat

events.title: The law separating the Churches and the State, 9 December 1905
events.summary: After years of conflict between the Republic and the Catholic Church, Parliament ends the Concordat of 1801. The Republic guarantees freedom of conscience and of worship, but no longer recognises or pays any religion. Church buildings become public property, left for the use of the faithful. The law founds French laïcité. Alsace and Moselle, then German, keep the Concordat to this day.
events.search: 1905 law separation of the Churches and the State laïcité France Concordat

events.title: The Tangier Crisis and the Algeciras Conference, 1905 – 1906
events.summary: On 31 March 1905, Kaiser Wilhelm II lands at Tangier and declares his support for the independence of Morocco, to test the new Entente between France and Britain. War seems possible, and France's foreign minister Delcassé has to resign. At the Algeciras conference in 1906, the powers keep Morocco formally independent but give France and Spain the policing of its ports and a hold on its finances. Britain stands by France, and Germany comes out isolated.
events.search: First Moroccan Crisis Tangier 1905 Wilhelm II Algeciras Conference 1906

events.title: The bombardment of Casablanca, August 1907
events.summary: In July 1907, Moroccans opposed to the French-run works at the port of Casablanca kill nine European workers. On 5 August French warships shell the city and troops land; the city is looted and thousands of Moroccans die. France then occupies the Chaouia plain around Casablanca, as it had occupied Oujda, on the Algerian border, in March. These are the first steps of the French conquest of Morocco.
events.search: Bombardment of Casablanca 1907 Chaouia occupation Oujda

events.title: Gouraud takes the Adrar, 1909
events.summary: After Coppolani's death, the emirate of Adrar and the followers of the religious leader Ma al-Aynayn lead the resistance in the north of Mauritania, with help from Morocco. Colonel Henri Gouraud marches a column across the desert and takes Atar in January 1909, then Chinguetti. The emir of Adrar submits, and by 1912 France has put down the last resistance in the Adrar.
events.search: Gouraud Adrar 1909 Atar Chinguetti Ma al-Aynayn conquest Mauritania

events.title: The conquest of Ouaddai, 1909 – 1911
events.summary: The sultanate of Ouaddai, east of Lake Chad, is the strongest state left in the region, living from the caravan trade across the Sahara. French troops take its capital Abéché in June 1909, but Sultan Dud Murra fights on with the help of the neighbouring sultanates of Dar Masalit and Dar Sila, which kill a French colonel at Doroté in 1910. Dud Murra surrenders in October 1911, and Ouaddai becomes part of French Chad.
events.search: Wadai War Ouaddai 1909 1911 Abeche Dud Murra conquest of Chad

events.title: The Agadir Crisis and the Morocco–Congo Treaty, 1911
events.summary: In May 1911 French troops march into Fez to help the Sultan against a revolt. Germany answers by sending the gunboat Panther to Agadir on 1 July, and Europe fears war. By the treaty of 4 November 1911, Germany accepts that France can make Morocco a protectorate. In return, France cedes to German Kamerun about 275,000 km² of its Equatorial Africa, Neukamerun, and gets a small strip south of Fort-Lamy, the Bec de canard.
events.search: Agadir Crisis 1911 Panther Morocco-Congo Treaty Neukamerun Bec de canard

events.title: The Treaty of Fes and the Fez riots, 1912
events.summary: On 30 March 1912, Sultan Abd al-Hafid signs the Treaty of Fes, making Morocco a French protectorate. Three weeks later, Moroccan soldiers in Fez mutiny, and with the townspeople kill French officers and civilians and attack the Jewish quarter. General Lyautey, the first resident-general, retakes the city and the surrounding region. The Sultan abdicates in August, and in November France gives Spain a zone in the north of Morocco.
events.search: Treaty of Fes 1912 French protectorate Morocco Fez riots Lyautey Abd al-Hafid

events.title: Brazza's treaty with King Makoko, 1880
events.summary: On 10 September 1880 the explorer Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza signs a treaty with Makoko, king of the Teke, who places his lands on the north bank of the Congo under French protection. Brazza founds a post on the river that will become Brazzaville. The French parliament ratifies the treaty in 1882, the start of French Congo.
events.search: Makoko treaty 1880 Brazza Teke Brazzaville French Congo

events.title: The Treaty of Bardo, 1881
events.summary: In April 1881, using raids by Khroumir tribesmen into Algeria as a pretext, French troops enter Tunisia. On 12 May, with soldiers around his palace, Muhammad III as-Sadiq Bey signs the Treaty of Bardo: France takes charge of Tunisia's army and foreign affairs. The 1883 La Marsa Convention completes the protectorate, which lasts until 1956.
events.search: Treaty of Bardo 1881 Tunisia French protectorate Khroumir Sadiq Bey La Marsa

events.title: The Tonkin campaign and the Sino-French War, 1883 – 1885
events.summary: France sends troops to Tonkin, and in August 1883 the Harmand treaty forces the court of Huế to accept a protectorate over Annam and Tonkin. China, which considers Vietnam its tributary, fights back with its armies and the Black Flags. After battles around Lạng Sơn and a French naval campaign off Fuzhou and Taiwan, the Treaty of Tientsin of June 1885 makes China give up its claims.
events.search: Sino-French War 1883 1885 Tonkin campaign Harmand treaty Lang Son Black Flags Tientsin

events.title: The Cần Vương revolt, 1885 – 1896
events.summary: In July 1885 the regent Tôn Thất Thuyết attacks the French garrison of Huế, then flees with the young emperor Hàm Nghi and calls on the Vietnamese to rise to "save the king" (Cần Vương). Scholars lead uprisings across Annam. Hàm Nghi is captured in 1888 and exiled to Algeria, and the last leader, Phan Đình Phùng, dies in 1895; the revolt ends the following year.
events.search: Can Vuong revolt 1885 Ham Nghi Ton That Thuyet Hue Phan Dinh Phung

events.title: The Indochinese Union is founded, 1887
events.summary: On 17 October 1887 France joins the colony of Cochinchina and the protectorates of Cambodia, Annam and Tonkin under one governor-general: the Indochinese Union, or French Indochina. Laos is added in 1899 and Guangzhouwan in 1900. The capital, first Saigon, moves to Hanoi in 1902.
events.search: Indochinese Union 1887 French Indochina governor-general Cochinchina Cambodia Annam Tonkin

events.title: The conquest of Dahomey, 1892 – 1894
events.summary: After a first war in 1890 over the coast around Cotonou and Porto-Novo, Colonel Alfred-Amédée Dodds marches on the kingdom of Dahomey in 1892. King Béhanzin's army, with its women soldiers, is beaten in a series of battles, and Abomey falls in November. Béhanzin surrenders in January 1894 and is exiled to Martinique; Dahomey becomes a French colony.
events.search: Second Franco-Dahomean War 1892 Dodds Behanzin Abomey Dahomey conquest

events.title: The Franco-Siamese crisis, 1893
events.summary: France claims the lands east of the Mekong, held by Siam. After clashes in Laos, French gunboats force their way up the Chao Phraya to Bangkok in July 1893 and blockade the coast. By the treaty of 3 October 1893, Siam gives up all the left bank of the Mekong, which becomes French Laos.
events.search: Franco-Siamese War crisis 1893 Paknam incident Mekong left bank Laos treaty

events.title: The French take Timbuktu, 1893 – 1894
events.summary: In December 1893 a French flotilla on the Niger reaches Timbuktu, the old city of trade and learning, and a column under Colonel Bonnier occupies it. In January 1894 Tuareg fighters wipe out Bonnier's column at Tacoubao. Major Joffre, the future marshal, arrives overland in February and holds the city for French Sudan.
events.search: Timbuktu 1893 1894 French conquest Bonnier Joffre Tuareg Tacoubao

events.title: French West Africa is founded, 1895
events.summary: On 16 June 1895 France places Senegal, French Sudan, French Guinea and Ivory Coast under one governor-general in Saint-Louis: French West Africa. Dahomey joins in 1899, Mauritania, Upper Volta and Niger later. In 1902 the capital moves to Dakar. The federation lasts until 1958.
events.search: French West Africa 1895 AOF founded governor-general Saint-Louis Dakar federation

events.title: The French conquest of Madagascar, 1895 – 1897
events.summary: In 1895 a French expedition lands at Mahajanga and marches inland; thousands of its soldiers die of fever on the way. Antananarivo is shelled and surrenders on 30 September, and the Merina kingdom accepts a protectorate. France annexes Madagascar in August 1896, and after a rising against French rule, General Gallieni exiles Queen Ranavalona III in February 1897 and ends the monarchy.
events.search: Second Franco-Hova War 1895 Madagascar expedition Antananarivo annexation 1896 Gallieni Ranavalona III exile

events.title: The capture of Samori Touré, 1898
events.summary: For almost twenty years Samori Touré, founder of the Wassoulou Empire around Bissandougou, fights the French advance in the upper Niger lands, moving his whole state east into the north of Ivory Coast in the 1890s. Surprised at Guélémou on 29 September 1898, he is captured and exiled to Gabon, where he dies in 1900. His lands are shared between French Guinea, French Sudan and Ivory Coast.
events.search: Samori Toure 1898 captured Guelemou Wassoulou Empire Bissandougou exile Gabon

events.title: The Voulet–Chanoine Mission, 1899
events.summary: Sent from French Sudan to reach Lake Chad, the column of Captains Paul Voulet and Julien Chanoine loots and burns villages across what is now Niger, killing thousands; at Birni-N'Konni in May 1899 most of the town's people are massacred. When Colonel Klobb is sent to take over, Voulet has him shot in July; their own soldiers then kill Voulet and Chanoine. The rest of the column reaches Zinder and Lake Chad.
events.search: Voulet-Chanoine Mission 1899 Birni N'Konni massacre Klobb Niger Zinder

events.title: Nice and Savoy join France, 1860
events.summary: In return for helping Piedmont-Sardinia against Austria in 1859, Napoleon III asks for Savoy and the County of Nice. By the Treaty of Turin of 24 March 1860, King Victor Emmanuel II cedes them, and plebiscites in April approve with huge majorities. France takes over on 14 June 1860. In 1861 the Prince of Monaco also sells Menton and Roquebrune to France.
events.search: Treaty of Turin 1860 Nice Savoy annexation plebiscite Napoleon III Cavour Menton Roquebrune

events.title: The French expedition to Lebanon, 1860 – 1861
events.summary: In 1860 fighting between Druze and Maronite Christians in Mount Lebanon turns into massacres, which spread to Damascus. With the agreement of the other European powers, Napoleon III sends some 6,000 soldiers, who land at Beirut in August 1860 and stay until June 1861. The Ottoman government then makes Mount Lebanon a self-governing district under a Christian governor.
events.search: 1860 Mount Lebanon civil war Druze Maronite massacres Damascus French expedition Beirut Mutasarrifate

events.title: The conquest of Cochinchina and the Treaty of Saigon, 1861 – 1862
events.summary: French and Spanish troops have held Saigon since 1859. In February 1861 they break the Vietnamese lines at Kỳ Hòa, then take Mỹ Tho and Biên Hòa. By the Treaty of Saigon of 5 June 1862, Emperor Tự Đức cedes the three eastern provinces of the south and Côn Sơn island to France, opens ports to trade and allows Catholic missions.
events.search: Cochinchina campaign 1861 1862 Ky Hoa Treaty of Saigon Tu Duc Bien Hoa Gia Dinh Dinh Tuong

events.title: The French intervention in Mexico, 1861 – 1867
events.summary: After Mexico stops paying its foreign debts, France, Britain and Spain land at Veracruz in December 1861. Britain and Spain soon leave, but Napoleon III wants a friendly empire in the Americas. Beaten at Puebla on 5 May 1862, the French take Mexico City in 1863 and make the Austrian archduke Maximilian emperor. Under pressure from the United States and Benito Juárez's republicans, the French leave in 1867, and Maximilian is shot at Querétaro.

events.title: Cambodia becomes a French protectorate, 1863
events.summary: Squeezed between Siam and Vietnam, King Norodom signs a treaty with Admiral de La Grandière on 11 August 1863 placing Cambodia under French protection. Siam, which had crowned Norodom, accepts it in 1867 in return for keeping Battambang and Siem Reap. The capital moves to Phnom Penh in 1866.

events.title: France takes western Cochinchina, 1867
events.summary: In June 1867 Admiral de La Grandière seizes the three western provinces of the south, Vĩnh Long, An Giang and Hà Tiên, without a fight. The old viceroy Phan Thanh Giản, who had signed the 1862 treaty, takes poison. All of southern Vietnam is now the French colony of Cochinchina, which Vietnam recognises in 1874.

events.title: The opening of the Suez Canal, 1869
events.summary: Built by Ferdinand de Lesseps's French company with Egyptian labour and money from 1859, the canal between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea opens on 17 November 1869, with Empress Eugénie aboard the first ship. It cuts the sea route from Europe to India and the Far East by thousands of kilometres. Egypt's debts force it to sell its shares to Britain in 1875.

events.title: The Franco-Prussian War, 1870 – 1871
events.summary: France declares war on Prussia on 19 July 1870. The German armies win quickly: Napoleon III surrenders at Sedan on 2 September, and two days later the Republic is proclaimed in Paris. Paris is besieged from September and Metz falls in October. On 18 January 1871 the German Empire is proclaimed at Versailles, and Paris surrenders ten days later.
events.search: Franco-Prussian War 1870 1871 Sedan Napoleon III surrender siege of Paris Metz Versailles German Empire

events.title: The Treaty of Frankfurt: Alsace-Lorraine lost, 1871
events.summary: Signed on 10 May 1871, the peace treaty gives the new German Empire Alsace and the north-east of Lorraine with Metz, about 1.6 million people; France keeps Belfort. France must pay five billion francs, and German troops occupy the east until it is paid. Tens of thousands of Alsatians and Lorrainers choose French nationality and leave.
events.search: Treaty of Frankfurt 1871 Alsace-Lorraine annexed German Empire Metz Strasbourg Belfort indemnity

events.title: The Paris Commune, 1871
events.summary: On 18 March 1871 Paris rises against the government of Adolphe Thiers, which wants to take back the National Guard's cannons, and elects a revolutionary council, the Commune. The regular army retakes the city in the "Bloody Week" of 21–28 May; thousands of Communards are killed, and many more are jailed or deported to New Caledonia.
events.search: Paris Commune 1871 Bloody Week Thiers National Guard Communards Versailles

events.title: The Mokrani revolt, 1871 – 1872
events.summary: In March 1871, as France is weakened by its defeat, Cheikh El Mokrani and the Rahmaniyya brotherhood call a rising in Kabylia and eastern Algeria, joined by some 250 tribes. El Mokrani is killed in May and the revolt is crushed by early 1872. The Kabyles are made to pay a huge fine and lose hundreds of thousands of hectares, given to settlers, many from Alsace-Lorraine.
events.search: Mokrani Revolt 1871 1872 Kabylia El Mokrani Rahmaniyya Algeria land confiscation

events.title: Garnier's Tonkin expedition, 1873
events.summary: Sent from Saigon to settle a dispute over trade on the Red River, the naval officer Francis Garnier storms the citadel of Hanoi on 20 November 1873 with about 200 men, then takes the forts of the delta. On 21 December he is killed near Hanoi by the Black Flags. Paris disowns the venture, and by the Treaty of Saigon of March 1874 the French leave Tonkin.

events.title: The end of the German occupation, 1873
events.summary: France pays the five-billion-franc war indemnity well ahead of schedule, thanks to two huge public loans in 1871 and 1872. German troops leave the occupied departments one by one, and on 16 September 1873 the last of them march out of Verdun. Thiers, who arranged the payment, is hailed as the "liberator of the territory".

events.title: The Kanak revolt in New Caledonia, 1878
events.summary: Driven off their land by settlers' cattle and the penal colony, Kanak clans led by the high chief Ataï rise in June 1878 around La Foa and Bouloupari, killing some 200 settlers. French troops, helped by rival clans, put down the revolt by early 1879. Ataï is killed in September 1878 and his head sent to Paris; about 1,000 Kanaks die and many more lose their land.

events.title: The Battle of Isly, 1844
events.summary: Morocco's sultan Abd al-Rahman shelters Abd al-Qadir, who leads the fight against the French in Algeria, and gathers an army on the border. On 14 August 1844 Marshal Bugeaud beats it on the Isly river near Oujda, while the French navy shells Tangier and Mogador. By the Treaty of Tangier in September, Morocco stops helping Abd al-Qadir, and the border with Algeria is drawn in 1845.

events.title: The Franco-Tahitian War, 1844 – 1847
events.summary: In 1843 Admiral Dupetit-Thouars deposes Queen Pōmare IV, who had accepted a French protectorate the year before, and she flees to Raiatea. Tahitians rise in 1844 and fight a guerrilla war from the island's valleys until their last stronghold, Fautaua, falls in December 1846. Pōmare returns in 1847 and rules under the protectorate; the Leeward Islands stay independent.

events.title: The surrender of Abd al-Qadir, 1847
events.summary: For fifteen years the emir Abd al-Qadir leads the fight against the French conquest of western Algeria, with a state of his own and a moving capital, the Smala. Hunted down and no longer welcome in Morocco, he surrenders to General Lamoricière on 23 December 1847. Promised exile in the East, he is instead held in France until 1852, and later lives in Damascus.

events.title: The Revolution of 1848 and the end of slavery
events.summary: In February 1848 Parisians rise against King Louis-Philippe, who abdicates, and the Second Republic is proclaimed. Men get the vote, and on 27 April a decree drafted by Victor Schœlcher abolishes slavery in all French colonies, freeing some 250,000 people in the Caribbean, Réunion and Senegal. In December Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte is elected president.

events.title: Napoleon III's coup and the Second Empire, 1851 – 1852
events.summary: Barred from a second term, President Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte dissolves the Assembly on 2 December 1851, the anniversary of Austerlitz. Risings in Paris and the provinces are put down and thousands are deported, many to Algeria. A year later, on 2 December 1852, after a plebiscite, he becomes Emperor Napoleon III.

events.title: France annexes New Caledonia, 1853
events.summary: Looking for a site for a penal colony in the Pacific, Napoleon III sends Admiral Febvrier-Despointes, who takes possession of New Caledonia at Balade on 24 September 1853. Port-de-France, later Nouméa, is founded in 1854. From 1864 convicts are sent there, and the Kanak people lose much of their land to settlers.

events.title: The Crimean War, 1853 – 1856
events.summary: Russia attacks the Ottoman Empire in 1853, and France and Britain join the Ottomans in 1854, later helped by Sardinia. The allies land in Crimea and besiege the Russian naval base of Sevastopol for almost a year, until the French take the Malakoff fort in September 1855. About 95,000 French soldiers die, mostly of disease. The Treaty of Paris of 1856 closes the Black Sea to warships.

events.title: Faidherbe in Senegal and the siege of Médine, 1854 – 1857
events.summary: Made governor of Senegal in 1854, Louis Faidherbe pushes French rule up the Senegal river, beats the Trarza emirate and builds forts, including Médine in 1855. In April 1857 the army of El Hadj Umar Tall, who is building an empire on the upper Niger, besieges Médine for three months, until Faidherbe relieves it on 18 July. The same year France occupies Dakar and Faidherbe raises the Senegalese Tirailleurs.

events.title: The conquest of Kabylia, 1857
events.summary: The mountains of Greater Kabylia, east of Algiers, are the last part of northern Algeria outside French rule. In May 1857 Marshal Randon leads some 35,000 men into them and, after hard fighting at Icheriden, the villages submit by July. Lalla Fatma N'Soumer, who had led the resistance, is captured. The French build Fort-Napoléon, now Larbaâ Nath Irathen, to hold the region.

events.title: The siege of Tourane and the capture of Saigon, 1858 – 1860
events.summary: To stop the persecution of Catholic missionaries and gain a foothold in Asia, a French and Spanish fleet under Admiral Rigault de Genouilly attacks Tourane, now Da Nang, on 1 September 1858. Stuck there by Vietnamese resistance and disease, the admiral sails south and takes the citadel of Saigon on 17 February 1859. Tourane is given up in March 1860, but Saigon is held.

events.title: Magenta and Solferino: the war for Italy, 1859
events.summary: Allied to Piedmont-Sardinia, Napoleon III goes to war with Austria in April 1859 and leads the French army into Lombardy himself. The French and Sardinians win at Magenta on 4 June and at Solferino on 24 June, one of the bloodiest battles of the century, whose horrors lead Henry Dunant to found the Red Cross. Lombardy passes to Sardinia, and in return France receives Nice and Savoy in 1860.

events.title: Waterloo and the second Treaty of Paris, 1815
events.summary: Back from Elba for a Hundred Days, Napoleon is beaten at Waterloo on 18 June 1815 by Wellington's British, Dutch and German army and Blücher's Prussians. He abdicates again and is sent to Saint Helena, and Louis XVIII returns to Paris on 8 July. By the second Treaty of Paris of 20 November 1815, France loses Landau, Saarlouis, Philippeville and the part of Savoy it had kept in 1814, must pay 700 million francs and accept an army of occupation.

events.title: The end of the Allied occupation, 1818
events.summary: Since 1815 an Allied army of 150,000 men under Wellington, with headquarters at Cambrai, has held the north-east of France as a guarantee for the war indemnity. Thanks to loans from the Baring and Hope banks, the Duke of Richelieu's government pays early, and at the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle in October 1818 the powers agree to leave. The last troops are gone by the end of November, and France joins the Concert of Europe.

events.title: Radama I and the Merina conquest of Madagascar, 1817 – 1828
events.summary: King Radama I of Imerina signs a treaty with Britain in October 1817, ending the slave trade in return for weapons and advisers, and Britain recognises him as King of Madagascar. With a modern army he takes Tamatave and the east coast, then Mahajanga and the north-west in 1824, and Fort-Dauphin in 1825. By his death in 1828 the Merina rule about two-thirds of the island, but never the Sakalava west or the far south.

events.title: The French invasion of Algiers, 1830
events.summary: Using a quarrel with the Dey of Algiers, who had struck the French consul with a fly whisk in 1827, Charles X's government sends 37,000 men, who land at Sidi Ferruch on 14 June 1830. Algiers surrenders on 5 July and the Dey goes into exile, ending three centuries of Ottoman rule. Charles X falls weeks later, but the July Monarchy keeps the city and slowly extends the conquest.

events.title: The July Revolution, 1830
events.summary: When Charles X suspends press freedom and dissolves the newly elected Chamber, Parisians build barricades and fight the army for three days, the "Three Glorious Days" of 27–29 July 1830. Charles X abdicates and leaves for exile, and the liberal deputies offer the crown to his cousin Louis-Philippe, Duke of Orléans, who becomes King of the French on 9 August: the July Monarchy begins.

events.title: Egypt rules Syria, 1831 – 1840
events.summary: Muhammad Ali, the Ottoman governor of Egypt, sends his son Ibrahim Pasha to take Syria in 1831. Acre falls in May 1832, Damascus soon after, and Ibrahim beats the Sultan's armies at Homs and Konya. Egypt rules Syria and Lebanon for eight years, until Britain, Austria and Russia step in during the Oriental Crisis of 1840: Acre is shelled and Ibrahim withdraws, while France, which backed Muhammad Ali, is left out.

events.title: The Treaty of Tafna, 1837
events.summary: On 30 May 1837 General Bugeaud signs a treaty with the emir Abd al-Qadir on the Tafna river. France keeps Algiers, Oran and the coast around them, and recognises the emir's rule over most of western and central Algeria, including Tlemcen. Abd al-Qadir uses the truce to build up his state, until the French march through his land in 1839 and the war starts again.

events.title: The siege of Constantine, 1837
events.summary: After a failed attack in 1836, a French army of 20,000 under General Damrémont returns to Constantine, the stronghold of Ahmed Bey on its rocky gorge. Damrémont is killed by a cannonball on 12 October 1837, and the next day General Valée's troops storm the breach and take the city after hard street fighting. Ahmed Bey holds out in the Aurès until 1848.

events.title: The Republic is proclaimed, 4 September 1870
events.summary: Two days after Napoleon III's surrender at Sedan, crowds invade the Assembly and Léon Gambetta proclaims the Republic at the Hôtel de Ville of Paris. A Government of National Defence carries on the war against Prussia. The Third Republic that follows lasts until 1940, the longest French regime since the Revolution.

events.title: De Gaulle's Provisional Government, 1944 – 1946
events.summary: On 3 June 1944, in Algiers, the French Committee of National Liberation makes itself the Provisional Government of the French Republic, led by Charles de Gaulle. It moves to Paris after the liberation in August, sweeping away the Vichy regime, and gives women the vote. De Gaulle resigns in January 1946, and the Fourth Republic begins that October.

events.title: Dom Miguel seizes the throne: the Liberal Wars, 1828 – 1834
events.summary: In July 1828 Dom Miguel, regent for his niece Maria II, has himself proclaimed absolute king and tears up the liberal Charter. His brother Pedro, emperor of Brazil, abdicates there and lands near Porto in 1832 to fight for his daughter. After two years of civil war the Miguelists surrender at Évora-Monte in May 1834, and Maria II rules as a constitutional queen.

events.title: Sidónio Pais's coup, 1917
events.summary: With Portugal worn down by its part in the First World War, Major Sidónio Pais leads a military revolt in Lisbon on 5–8 December 1917 and overthrows Afonso Costa's government. He rules as a presidential dictator, the "New Republic", until he is shot dead at Rossio station on 14 December 1918.

events.title: Boumediène's coup, 1965

events.title: Tunisia becomes a republic, 1957

events.title: The Anglo-Egyptian condominium over the Sudan, 19 January 1899
events.summary: After the reconquest, Britain and Egypt sign an agreement on 19 January 1899 to rule the Sudan jointly. Both flags fly, but a British governor-general holds all power, and Kitchener is the first. The condominium sets the 22nd parallel as the Sudan’s northern border and lasts until independence on 1 January 1956.

events.title: The Anglo-Kuwaiti Agreement, 23 January 1899
events.summary: Fearing that the Ottomans would make good their claims – and that Germany would end its Baghdad railway at Kuwait – Sheikh Mubarak al-Sabah signs a secret bond with Britain on 23 January 1899. He promises not to cede land or receive foreign agents without British consent, in return for British protection. Kuwait stays under that protection until its independence in 1961.

events.title: The Basotho Gun War and the return of direct British rule, 1880 – 1884
events.summary: When the Cape Colony, which had run Basutoland since 1871, orders the Basotho to hand in their guns, they rise in September 1880 and fight the Cape forces to a standstill. The Cape gives up, and on 18 March 1884 Britain takes Basutoland back under direct rule from London. This kept it out of South Africa and is why Lesotho is an independent country today.

events.title: The battle of Tel el-Kebir and the British occupation of Egypt, 13 September 1882
events.summary: After the nationalist army officer Ahmed Urabi takes power and riots break out in Alexandria, the Royal Navy bombards the city in July 1882 and a British army lands by the Suez Canal. Garnet Wolseley’s dawn attack routs Urabi’s army at Tel el-Kebir on 13 September, and Cairo falls the next day. The khedive is restored under British control, and British troops stay in Egypt for 74 years.

events.title: The fall of Khartoum and the death of Gordon, 26 January 1885
events.summary: Sent to evacuate the Egyptian garrisons from a Sudan overrun by the Mahdi’s rising, General Charles Gordon instead holds Khartoum through a ten-month siege. The Mahdists storm the city on 26 January 1885 and kill Gordon, two days before a British relief force arrives. Egypt gives up the Sudan, and the Mahdi’s successor rules it from Omdurman until 1898.

events.title: Britain declares the Bechuanaland Protectorate, 31 March 1885
events.summary: To keep the Boer republics and German South West Africa from joining up, and to hold the “road to the north”, Britain sends the Warren Expedition and declares a protectorate over the Tswana lands on 31 March 1885. The south becomes British Bechuanaland, later joined to the Cape, while the north stays a protectorate. In 1895 the chiefs Khama III, Sebele and Bathoen go to London to keep it out of Cecil Rhodes’s company. It becomes independent Botswana in 1966.

events.title: The Third Anglo-Burmese War: Upper Burma annexed, November 1885 – January 1886
events.summary: Fearing French influence at the court of King Thibaw and angered by a fine on a British timber company, Britain sends a river fleet up the Irrawaddy in November 1885. Mandalay falls on 28 November almost without a fight, and Thibaw is exiled to India. On 1 January 1886 Upper Burma is annexed and the whole country becomes a province of British India, ending the Konbaung dynasty; resistance goes on for years.

events.summary: George Goldie’s National African Company, which had bought out its French rivals on the Niger and signed hundreds of treaties with local rulers, is chartered as the Royal Niger Company on 10 July 1886. It governs the lower and middle Niger and Benue, with a monopoly on trade, and fights the emirates of Bida and Ilorin. In 1900 the Crown takes over its lands, which become the heart of Northern and Southern Nigeria.

events.title: North Borneo, Sarawak and Brunei become British protectorates, 1888
events.summary: To shut out other powers, Britain makes protectorates of the three states of northern Borneo in 1888: the British North Borneo Company’s lands in May, the Brooke family’s Raj of Sarawak in June and the Sultanate of Brunei in September. Britain takes their foreign affairs while each keeps its own rulers. Sarawak and North Borneo join Malaysia in 1963; Brunei stays apart and becomes independent in 1984.

events.summary: Tibetan troops fortify the Jelep La route at Lingtu, inside Sikkim, in 1886. In 1888 a British Indian force drives them out and defeats them at Gnatong in September. events.title: The Third Anglo-Ashanti War and the Gold Coast Colony, 1873 – 1874
events.summary: After Britain buys the Dutch forts, among them Elmina, in 1872, the Asante kingdom, which claimed Elmina, invades the coast. Garnet Wolseley marches inland, burns Kumasi in February 1874, and the Treaty of Fomena makes Asante give up its claims to the south. On 24 July 1874 the coastal lands become the Gold Coast Colony, the core of today’s Ghana.

events.summary: To end the Larut wars between Chinese tin-mining societies and a disputed succession in Perak, the governor of the Straits Settlements, Andrew Clarke, has the chiefs sign a treaty on Pangkor island on 20 January 1874. events.summary: The slave-trader and warlord al-Zubayr Rahma Mansur, master of the Bahr el Ghazal, invades Darfur from the south. Sultan Ibrahim is killed at the battle of Manawashi in October 1874, and in November Zubayr and the Khedive’s troops take El Fasher. Darfur becomes a province of the Egyptian Sudan until the Mahdists take it in 1883; its sultanate is restored in 1898 under Ali Dinar.

events.summary: Close to bankruptcy, Khedive Ismail sells Egypt’s 44% stake in the Suez Canal Company. Prime Minister Benjamin Disraeli buys it for Britain in November 1875 for four million pounds lent by the Rothschilds, without waiting for Parliament. Britain now owns a large share of its route to India, and its stake in Egypt’s finances leads to the occupation of 1882.

events.summary: The first British Resident of Perak, James Birch, angers the chiefs by taking over tax collection and pressing reforms. On 2 November 1875 he is killed at Pasir Salak on the orders of the Maharaja Lela. British and Indian troops occupy Perak; the Maharaja Lela is hanged and Sultan Abdullah exiled to the Seychelles. British control over the state is firmer than before.

events.summary: Robert Sandeman, sent to settle quarrels between the Khan of Kalat and his Baloch chiefs, brings them to sign the Treaty of Jacobabad on 8 December 1876. The khanate keeps its ruler but comes under British protection, and British troops may be stationed in it; Quetta, guarding the Bolan Pass toward Afghanistan, becomes a British base. The Viceroy, Lord Lytton, proclaims it before the princes of India at a vast Imperial Assemblage in Delhi on 1 January 1877, even as famine spreads in the south. events.summary: In a secret convention of 4 June 1878, the Ottoman sultan lets Britain occupy and govern Cyprus in return for a British promise to defend his Asian lands against Russia. British troops land and Garnet Wolseley takes over the government in July 1878, while the island stays Ottoman in name and pays tribute. Britain annexes it in 1914, when the Ottomans join Germany in the First World War.

events.summary: When Emir Sher Ali receives a Russian mission but turns a British one back, British Indian armies invade Afghanistan in November 1878. After the British envoy is killed in Kabul the war starts again; it ends in 1880 with Abdur Rahman as emir and the British back behind the new frontier, now holding Pishin and Sibi.

events.summary: At the end of the Second Opium War, after British and French troops take Beijing and burn the Old Summer Palace, Prince Gong signs the Convention of Peking with Lord Elgin on 24 October 1860. China cedes to Britain the tip of the Kowloon peninsula, south of today’s Boundary Street, with Stonecutters Island, facing Hong Kong Island across the harbour. events.summary: After raids into British Darjeeling and the seizure of two British doctors, a British force marches into Sikkim. On 28 March 1861, at the capital Tumlong, the Sikkimese court signs a treaty that opens the country to British trade and roads to Tibet and puts it under British protection. Sikkim stays a protectorate, of Britain and then of India, until it becomes an Indian state in 1975.

events.title: The Indian Rebellion, 1857 – 1858
events.summary: On 10 May 1857 sepoys at Meerut mutiny over greased cartridges and years of grievances, march to Delhi and proclaim the old Mughal emperor Bahadur Shah Zafar their leader. The revolt spreads across the Ganges plain and central India, with sieges and massacres at Cawnpore and Lucknow. British and loyal Indian troops retake Delhi in September 1857 and crush the last fighters in 1858; the Mughal empire ends, and so does the East India Company’s rule.

events.summary: After the rebellion, Parliament passes the Government of India Act on 2 August 1858, and the East India Company hands its Indian lands, army and officials to the Crown. events.summary: On 19 August 1991 hardliners of the Communist Party and the KGB hold Mikhail Gorbachev at his dacha in Crimea and declare a state of emergency, to stop a new union treaty that would loosen the Soviet Union. events.summary: The "Stalin Constitution" adopted on 5 December 1936 raises the number of union republics from seven to eleven. The Kazakh and Kirghiz autonomous republics leave the Russian SFSR to become the Kazakh and Kirghiz SSRs, Karakalpakstan moves to the Uzbek SSR, and the Transcaucasian SFSR is split into the Georgian, Armenian and Azerbaijan SSRs. events.title: Finland declares independence, 6 December 1917
events.summary: A month after the Bolsheviks take power in Petrograd, the Finnish Senate led by Pehr Evind Svinhufvud declares the Grand Duchy, part of the Russian Empire since 1809, an independent state on 6 December 1917. It gives up Poland, the Baltic lands and Finland, recognises Ukraine, and hands Kars, Ardahan and Batumi to the Ottomans: a third of the old empire's people. Germany's defeat in November 1918 voids the treaty, but most of the lost western lands never come back.

events.summary: By the Treaty of Neuilly of November 1919 Bulgaria gives up Western Thrace to the Allies, who run it for a few months under a French general. Greek troops move in on 14 May 1920, and Bulgaria loses its outlet on the Aegean.

events.title: Greece becomes a republic, March 1924
events.summary: After the defeat in Asia Minor and the officers' revolt of 1922, King George II is sent into exile. On 25 March 1924 Parliament proclaims the Second Hellenic Republic, confirmed by a referendum in April.

events.title: The Greek monarchy is restored, 1935
events.summary: In October 1935 General Georgios Kondylis seizes power and abolishes the republic. A rigged referendum on 3 November brings back King George II, who in August 1936 lets Ioannis Metaxas rule as dictator.

events.title: Greece under Axis occupation, 1941 – 1944
events.summary: Germany invades in April 1941 to rescue the Italians, held back by the Greeks since October 1940, and takes Crete in May. Greece is shared out: Germany keeps Athens, Thessaloniki, Crete and the islands facing Turkey, Italy most of the rest, Bulgaria eastern Macedonia and Thrace. Famine and resistance follow until the Germans leave in October 1944.

events.title: The Dodecanese pass to Greece, 1947
events.summary: Italian since 1912 and held by the British after the German surrender of May 1945, the Dodecanese are given to Greece by the Paris peace treaty with Italy of February 1947. The British hand them over on 31 March 1947, and they are formally joined to Greece in March 1948.
events.search: Dodecanese to Greece 31 March 1947 British military administration Paris Peace Treaty Italy 10 February 1947 Rhodes union 7 March 1948

events.title: The colonels' junta rules Greece, 1967 – 1974
events.summary: On 21 April 1967 a group of colonels led by Georgios Papadopoulos seizes power. King Constantine II fails to overthrow them and goes into exile; the junta abolishes the monarchy on 1 June 1973. It falls in July 1974 after the Turkish invasion of Cyprus, and a referendum in December confirms the republic.

events.title: The Treaty of Adrianople and the Russian protectorate over the principalities, 1829
events.summary: Russian troops had occupied Moldavia and Wallachia since 1828. By the Treaty of Adrianople of 14 September 1829 the Ottomans give the Danube delta to Russia and hand the fortresses of Brăila, Giurgiu and Turnu back to Wallachia. The principalities stay under the sultan but become a Russian protectorate, run by the Russian general Pavel Kiselyov until 1834.

events.title: The Wallachian revolution and its suppression, 1848
events.summary: In June 1848 liberal revolutionaries take power in Bucharest and drive out the prince. In September Ottoman and Russian troops enter Wallachia and put down the revolution; by the Convention of Balta Liman both powers keep troops in the two principalities until 1851.
events.search: Wallachian Revolution 1848 Islaz proclamation provisional government Bucharest Russian and Ottoman intervention September 1848 Balta Liman 1849 occupation until 1851

events.title: Moldavia and Wallachia unite under Alexandru Ioan Cuza, 1859
events.summary: The Great Powers had allowed each principality its own prince. Moldavia elects Alexandru Ioan Cuza in January 1859, and on 5 February Wallachia elects him too, uniting the two under one ruler. The United Principalities take the name Romania in 1862, with Bucharest as capital, still under Ottoman suzerainty.
events.search: Union of the Principalities 1859 Alexandru Ioan Cuza elected Moldavia 17 January Wallachia 5 February United Principalities Romania 1862 Bucharest capital

events.title: The Russo-Turkish War in Bulgaria, 1877 – 1878
events.summary: After the Ottomans crush the April Uprising in Bulgaria, Russia declares war in April 1877 and crosses the Danube in June. Held up for months at Plevna, which falls to Russian and Romanian troops in December, the Russians then cross the Balkans in winter, take Sofia and Plovdiv, and reach the gates of Constantinople. The Treaty of San Stefano in March 1878 creates a large Bulgaria.

events.title: The Treaty of Berlin divides Bulgaria, July 1878
events.summary: The Great Powers cut down the large Bulgaria of San Stefano. North of the Balkan range the Principality of Bulgaria is created under Ottoman suzerainty; south of it, Eastern Rumelia becomes an autonomous Ottoman province, and Macedonia goes back to the sultan. Romania becomes independent and receives Northern Dobruja and the Danube delta.
events.search: Treaty of Berlin 13 July 1878 Principality of Bulgaria Eastern Rumelia autonomous Macedonia returned Romania independence Northern Dobruja San Stefano revised

events.title: Romania becomes a kingdom, 1881
events.summary: Romania had declared its independence in May 1877 and fought alongside Russia, and the Treaty of Berlin recognised it. On 26 March 1881 Parliament proclaims the Kingdom of Romania, and Prince Carol of Hohenzollern is crowned King Carol I in May.
events.search: Kingdom of Romania proclaimed 26 March 1881 Carol I crowned May 1881 independence 1877 Treaty of Berlin

events.title: Eastern Rumelia unites with Bulgaria, 1885
events.summary: On 18 September 1885 Bulgarian nationalists take power in Plovdiv without a shot and proclaim the union of Eastern Rumelia with Bulgaria. Prince Alexander accepts it, beats off a Serbian attack at Slivnitsa in November, and the sultan names him governor of Eastern Rumelia by the Tophane Agreement of 1886.

events.title: Bulgaria declares its independence, October 1908
events.summary: Taking advantage of the Young Turk revolution, Prince Ferdinand proclaims Bulgaria fully independent of the Ottoman Empire in the old capital Veliko Tarnovo on 5 October 1908, and takes the title of tsar.
events.search: Bulgarian Declaration of Independence 5 October 1908 Veliko Tarnovo Ferdinand tsar Kingdom of Bulgaria Ottoman suzerainty ended Bosnian crisis

events.title: The Central Powers overrun Wallachia and Dobruja, 1916
events.summary: Romania joins the Allies in August 1916 and invades Transylvania, but the Central Powers strike back. Bulgarian and German troops take Turtucaia and Constanța, and German armies cross the Carpathians and enter Bucharest on 6 December. Romania holds on in Moldavia, while Wallachia and Dobruja stay occupied until November 1918.

events.title: Southern Dobruja goes back to Bulgaria, September 1940
events.summary: Romania had held Southern Dobruja since 1913. Under German pressure, and after losing Bessarabia and northern Transylvania that summer, it gives the region back to Bulgaria by the Treaty of Craiova of 7 September 1940, with an exchange of populations.
events.search: Treaty of Craiova 7 September 1940 Southern Dobruja returned to Bulgaria Romania Quadrilateral population exchange Dobrich Silistra

events.title: Bulgaria becomes a people's republic, 1946
events.summary: Under Soviet occupation since 1944, Bulgaria votes to abolish the monarchy in a referendum on 8 September 1946. The nine-year-old Tsar Simeon II goes into exile, and the communist Georgi Dimitrov leads the new People's Republic, which lasts until 1990.
events.search: People's Republic of Bulgaria referendum 8 September 1946 monarchy abolished Simeon II exile 15 September Georgi Dimitrov communist 1990 Republic of Bulgaria

events.title: Italy invades Albania, April 1939
events.summary: On 7 April 1939 Italian troops land at Durrës and other ports and take Tirana within days. King Zog flees abroad, and a puppet assembly offers the crown to Victor Emmanuel III of Italy. Albania becomes an Italian protectorate, run by an Italian governor.
events.search: Italian invasion of Albania 7 April 1939 Durrës King Zog flees Victor Emmanuel III king of Albania protectorate Francesco Jacomoni

events.title: The Greek army pushes into southern Albania, 1940 – 1941
events.summary: Italy attacks Greece from Albania in October 1940, but the Greeks throw the invasion back and advance into Albania, taking Korçë on 22 November and Gjirokastër in December. They hold the south of the country through the winter, until the German invasion of Greece in April 1941 forces them to withdraw.

events.title: The Axis invades and carves up Yugoslavia, April 1941
events.summary: Germany, Italy and Hungary invade Yugoslavia on 6 April 1941, and its army surrenders on 17 April while the king and government go into exile. The country is carved up: Bosnia goes to the new Independent State of Croatia, Serbia is put under German military rule, Montenegro under Italy, most of Kosovo and western Macedonia are joined to Italian-ruled Albania, and Bulgaria takes the rest of Macedonia.

events.title: Germany takes over the Italian zones, September 1943
events.summary: When Italy surrenders on 8 September 1943, German troops disarm the Italian garrisons and occupy Albania, Montenegro, Kosovo and western Macedonia. In Albania they set up a nominally independent government under their control, until they withdraw in late 1944.
events.search: Italian armistice 8 September 1943 German occupation of Albania Montenegro Kosovo western Macedonia disarm Italian troops regency council

events.title: Belgrade is liberated, October 1944
events.summary: Bulgaria changes sides in September 1944 and its troops leave Serbia and Macedonia. Yugoslav Partisans and the Soviet Red Army then take Belgrade on 20 October, and the German army pulls out of Macedonia, Kosovo and Montenegro by the end of the year.
events.search: Belgrade offensive liberation 20 October 1944 Partisans Red Army Bulgaria changes sides September 1944 German withdrawal Macedonia Kosovo Montenegro

events.title: The communists take power in Albania, 1944 – 1946
events.summary: The communist-led partisans of Enver Hoxha take Tirana on 17 November 1944, and the last German troops leave Albania by 29 November. Hoxha's provisional government rules the country, which is proclaimed the People's Republic of Albania on 11 January 1946; the monarchy is abolished.

events.title: Yugoslavia becomes a federal people's republic, 1945
events.summary: After the Partisans' victory, the assembly elected in November 1945 abolishes the monarchy and on 29 November proclaims the Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia under Josip Broz Tito. It is a federation of six republics: Serbia, Croatia, Slovenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Macedonia, with Kosovo and Vojvodina as autonomous parts of Serbia.

events.title: Communist rule ends in Albania, 1991
events.summary: After student protests and mass flight abroad in 1990, Albania's communist rulers allow other parties. Following the first multi-party elections, the People's Socialist Republic becomes the Republic of Albania on 29 April 1991, and the Democratic Party wins power in 1992.

events.title: Macedonia leaves Yugoslavia, 1991
events.summary: In a referendum on 8 September 1991 Macedonia votes for independence from the breaking-up Yugoslavia. The Yugoslav army withdraws peacefully in early 1992, and the Republic of Macedonia joins the United Nations in 1993 under a provisional name because of a dispute with Greece.

events.title: Bosnia's independence and the Bosnian War, 1992 – 1995
events.summary: Bosnia and Herzegovina declares its independence from Yugoslavia on 3 March 1992. Bosnian Serb forces, backed by Belgrade, take most of the north and east for their self-proclaimed Republika Srpska, and Bosnian Croats set up Herzeg-Bosnia in the west. After the Washington Agreement of 1994 ends the Croat-Bosniak fighting, the Dayton Agreement of December 1995 ends the war and splits the country into two entities.

events.title: The Kosovo War and the UN administration, 1998 – 1999
events.summary: Fighting between the Kosovo Liberation Army and Serbian forces grows in 1998. After 78 days of NATO bombing from March 1999, Yugoslavia agrees to pull its forces out, and on 10 June UN Security Council Resolution 1244 puts Kosovo under a United Nations administration (UNMIK), while leaving it formally part of Serbia.

events.title: Yugoslavia becomes Serbia and Montenegro, 2003
events.summary: On 4 February 2003 the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, made up of Serbia and Montenegro since 1992, is turned into a looser State Union of Serbia and Montenegro, and the name Yugoslavia disappears. The new charter lets either republic leave after three years.

events.title: Montenegro and Serbia go their own ways, 2006
events.summary: In a referendum on 21 May 2006, 55.5 percent of Montenegrin voters choose independence, just above the 55 percent the European Union had required. Montenegro declares independence on 3 June, and Serbia becomes the successor of the State Union on 5 June.

events.title: Kosovo declares its independence, 2008
events.summary: On 17 February 2008 the Assembly of Kosovo declares independence from Serbia, ending nine years of United Nations administration. Many countries recognise the new republic, but Serbia, Russia and others do not; in 2010 the International Court of Justice finds that the declaration did not break international law.

events.title: Macedonia becomes North Macedonia, 2019
events.summary: The Prespa Agreement, signed with Greece in June 2018 on Lake Prespa, ends a 27-year dispute over the country's name. On 12 February 2019 the Republic of Macedonia becomes the Republic of North Macedonia, and Greece lifts its veto on its joining NATO, which it does in 2020.

events.title: Albania declares its independence, November 1912
events.summary: With Serbian, Montenegrin and Greek armies overrunning the Ottoman Balkans, Albanian delegates meet at Vlorë and on 28 November 1912 declare Albania independent, with Ismail Qemali at the head of a provisional government. For months it controls little more than the area around Vlorë.

events.title: The Treaty of London ends the First Balkan War, May 1913
events.summary: On 30 May 1913 the Ottoman Empire gives up all its European land west of a line from Enos to Midia, and Crete. Kosovo, the Sandžak and most of Macedonia are left to the Balkan allies who had taken them, and the Great Powers decide that Albania will be an independent principality.

events.title: Prince Wilhelm of Wied and the Principality of Albania, 1914
events.summary: The Great Powers choose a German prince, Wilhelm of Wied, as ruler of Albania. He lands at Durrës on 7 March 1914, but faces revolts and a Greek-backed uprising in the south, and leaves the country in September after the First World War breaks out.

events.title: The Central Powers overrun Serbia, October – December 1915
events.summary: In October 1915 German and Austro-Hungarian armies cross the Danube and take Belgrade, while Bulgaria attacks from the east. The Serbian army, with the king and government, retreats over the mountains of Kosovo and Albania to the Adriatic and is shipped to Corfu. Serbia is split into an Austro-Hungarian and a Bulgarian zone of occupation until 1918.

events.title: Austria-Hungary conquers Montenegro, January 1916
events.summary: In January 1916 Austro-Hungarian troops storm Mount Lovćen and take Cetinje. Montenegro capitulates, King Nicholas flees to Italy, and the country is ruled by an Austro-Hungarian military government until the autumn of 1918.
events.search: Montenegrin campaign January 1916 Mount Lovćen Cetinje falls capitulation King Nicholas exile Austro-Hungarian military governorate

events.title: Albania divided among the warring powers, 1914 – 1918
events.summary: Neutral Albania is soon occupied from every side. Italy lands at Vlorë in December 1914, and Montenegro takes Shkodër in 1915. In 1916 Austria-Hungary occupies the north and centre, Italy pushes into the south and France takes Korçë, where it sets up an autonomous Albanian republic. The front runs across the country until the autumn of 1918.

events.title: The Allies break through in Macedonia and free Serbia, 1918
events.summary: On 15 September 1918 Serbian and French troops break the Bulgarian front at Dobro Pole. Bulgaria signs the Armistice of Salonica on 29 September, and the Serbian army drives north through Macedonia, Kosovo and Serbia, retaking Niš in October and Belgrade on 1 November.

events.title: The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes is created, December 1918
events.summary: As Austria-Hungary collapses, its South Slav lands, including Bosnia, form a State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs in October 1918. In November an assembly at Podgorica deposes King Nicholas and votes to join Montenegro to Serbia. On 1 December 1918 Prince Regent Alexander proclaims the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes in Belgrade.

events.title: The Treaty of Neuilly cuts back Bulgaria, 1919
events.summary: By the Treaty of Neuilly of 27 November 1919 Bulgaria gives the Western Outlands around Caribrod and Bosilegrad and the Strumica valley to the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and Western Thrace to the Allies. The treaty comes into force on 9 August 1920.

events.title: Albania wins back its land: Lushnjë and the Vlora War, 1920
events.summary: In January 1920 the Congress of Lushnjë sets up a new Albanian government, which moves to Tirana. French troops leave Korçë in May, and in the summer Albanian fighters besiege the Italian garrison in Vlorë. By the Tirana protocol of 2 August Italy agrees to leave, keeping only the island of Sazan, and its last troops sail in September.

events.title: The Great Powers confirm Albania's borders, November 1921
events.summary: Yugoslav troops had held parts of northern Albania since 1918 and backed a breakaway Republic of Mirdita. On 9 November 1921 the Conference of Ambassadors confirms Albania's borders of 1913 with small changes, and under pressure from the League of Nations the Yugoslav army withdraws.

events.title: Albania becomes a republic under Ahmet Zogu, 1925
events.summary: After the June Revolution of 1924 put Fan Noli in power, Ahmet Zogu returns with Yugoslav backing in December. On 31 January 1925 Albania is proclaimed a republic, with Zogu as its president holding wide powers.

events.title: Zogu makes himself King Zog I, 1928
events.summary: On 1 September 1928 President Ahmet Zogu has the assembly proclaim Albania a kingdom and takes the title of Zog I, King of the Albanians. He rules until the Italian invasion of 1939, while Italy gains growing control over the country's economy.

events.title: King Alexander's dictatorship and the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, 1929
events.summary: After a deputy shoots Croatian leaders in parliament in 1928, King Alexander suspends the constitution on 6 January 1929 and rules as dictator. On 3 October he renames the country the Kingdom of Yugoslavia and redraws it into new provinces, the banovinas, cutting across the old historical lands.
